author: @kennethkuo9772
text:
Well done, Chase! You actually ended up at the China Square branch of Ya Kun Kaya Toast. There are countless outlets across the island for Ya Kun Kaya Toast, but the China Square branch is the one said to be still manned by the family/extended family members of the original founders, while all the other outlets are manned by hired staff and franchisees. Taste at this outlet is top notch and consistent!

Ah yes, Kaya is a wonderful food to bring back, if your home country allows bringing in for personal consumption. It goes well with most types of assorted breads and crackers! Most visitors would actually get some back for personal consumption. But just remember to keep it in the fridge once opened, till you finish the whole bottle. 👍

Best recommended way to eat the egg would be to mix the pepper and soya sauce well, and slurp it up. 

And yeah, we usually try not to dip kaya Toast in the coffee, as it will "disintegrate" very quickly.

Give you a hack for unusual way of having coffee.
We locals and Malaysians call it kopi gao gu you.
Or "butter coffee".
Simply, just order a cup of coffee like the Ya kun coffee (coffee with condensed milk) and drop a piece of BUTTER in the coffee. Preferably high quality butter like SCS or similar class you can find in your country, then wait for 2 to 3 minutes for the butter to slowly dissolve in the coffee while you sip up that heavenly taste of buttery coffee! Remember not to stir and dissolve the butter completely, as this will spread out the butter flavour all over. You let the butter dissolve naturally and you will have this distinctive taste that taste different with each mouthful. Cheers!

author: @Your.Uncle.AngMoh
text:
A Singaporean food vlogger (Dancing Bacons) called pandan "Asian vanilla" in a recent video. It's pretty horrid by itself, but it just adds so much to whatever it gets put into.

I was thinking that gula melaka would have been the sugar used historically. But the flavours in it would have quite an effect on the final taste of your kaya- and not necessarily for the better.

You don't mention pandan extract. Fresh is best, but sometimes one must make do with what one can get. It also, from my experience, tends to be coloured a very vivid artificial green.

Hot toast and cold butter combine really well. I was told as a kid to eat my crusts otherwise I wouldn't get curly hair. 

Add this dish of deliciousness to a couple of half-boiled eggs with white pepper and soy sauce. Wash it down with either a kopitiam coffee or a glass of sweet, black Cameron Highlands tea- teh O. This would be on high rotation for breakfast. One day this, the next a roti prata/canai, the next a Western/Singaporean scrambled eggs with turkey sausages and bacon (halal one!), and maybe a combination of what we in Australia call "Singapore noodles" and chicken curry on the fourth day. Fruit, cereal, and yoghurt would be for a brunch.

author: @wendythefoodscientist
text:
Recipe for homemade soy milk (2L) 🌱🥛
Ingredients:
- 200 g dried soybeans
- At least 600 ml water for soaking
- 2 L fresh water for blending

Method:

1️⃣ Rinse the soybeans well and soak them overnight in plenty of water. They should double in size.

2️⃣ Drain the soaked soybeans and blend them with 2 liters of water until smooth.

3️⃣ Strain the mixture through a cheesecloth or nut milk bag to separate the milk from the pulp.

4️⃣ Bring the strained soy milk to a gentle boil in a large saucepan.

5️⃣ Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring often to prevent sticking or burning. 

6️⃣ Let cool slightly. Serve fresh, or store in the fridge for up to 3–4 days. 🌿✨

✨ Bonus tip:

Save the okara (the leftover pulp)! It’s packed with fiber— perfect for cookies, banana bread, or savory fritters. Let me know if you want recipes.

text:
Deactivating anti-nutritional factors in soybeans through heat treatment

To make soybeans safe and digestible for consumption, it's crucial to apply proper heat treatment that deactivates their naturally occurring anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors (TIs), lectins, and urease, according to Anderson International Corp. However, finding the right balance between adequate heating and potential nutrient degradation (especially protein quality) is important. 

Here's a breakdown of common heat treatment methods and their impact:

1. Boiling

Soaking is crucial: Soaking soybeans for at least 8 hours (or even longer) before boiling is recommended to promote hydration and aid in inactivation.

Boiling time: Boiling the soaked beans for approximately 20 minutes can eliminate around 80% of the trypsin inhibitor activity. However, to achieve a soft texture similar to other cooked beans, you may need to boil for about 40 minutes. Extended boiling, like 60 minutes, is particularly effective for reducing tannins and phytic acids.

Protein quality: Boiling can cause some nutrient loss (e.g., vitamins) and can lead to a decrease in protein solubility, which might affect the functional properties of soy protein products. 

2. Pressure cooking

Time-saving: Pressure cooking significantly reduces cooking time while effectively inactivating anti-nutritional factors.

Soaked beans: Soaking beans for 1-4 hours before pressure cooking can be beneficial.

Cooking time: Pressure cooking times can range from 10-15 minutes for pre-soaked beans, and around 25 minutes if you skip the soaking step. 

3. Roasting

Effective for TIs and other ANFs: Roasting is effective in inactivating TIs, notes Wiley, and reducing other ANFs like tannins and phytic acid. Roasting at 180°C for 20 minutes can reduce TI activity by up to 90%.

Protein quality: Roasting might lead to some protein degradation, especially if temperatures are too high or the cooking time is extended. 

4. Microwaving

Speed and effectiveness: Microwaving offers a quick and relatively effective way to reduce TIs in soybeans, says Wiley Online Library.

Time: Microwaving for 3-4 minutes has been shown to be effective in reducing TI activity. 

Important considerations

Balancing heat and nutrition: While sufficient heat is needed to deactivate ANFs, overcooking can degrade protein quality, reduce the digestibility of amino acids (like lysine), and negatively impact other nutrients like heat-labile vitamins.

Monitoring trypsin inhibitor levels: For commercial processing, monitoring trypsin inhibitor levels is important, with a target of below 15,000 TI units per gram.

Different processing methods: The effectiveness of heat treatment can vary depending on the specific method used, the soybean variety, moisture content, and particle size. 

In essence, a combination of soaking and thorough cooking (boiling, pressure cooking, or other thermal treatments) is essential to deactivate harmful compounds in soybeans. Choose the cooking method that suits your needs, considering the desired texture and time constraints, while being mindful of not overcooking the soybeans to preserve their nutritional value.

text: Kaya is a coconut jam invented by the Hainanese migrants back in the days. Kaya means to stir the coconut in Hainanese dialect. Breads used to be toasted using charcoal. text:
When I was a kid, I would go 3 doors away to buy double slices of steamed white (or brown sometimes) bread with SCS butter and kaya (made by the coffeeshop). The coffeeshop would roast the coffee seeds spinning manually inside a big drum heated by fire wood, behind the back lane.

9-9.30pm, I would buy the same amount of bread from an elderly Punjabi man, who came on bicycle, carrying a big wooden box behind him. He would also give me some of the toasted slides especially the top layers. These toasted sides gave off a unique aroma when dipped into ovaltine or kopi O. However, bread back then, tasted very much better and they were heavier, than today. Today’s bread mostly are light weighted, don’t taste good and the texture becomes dry on the 2nd day.

Even as a local, I love ya kun (though it is pricey for just toast, eggs and coffee)
Ya kun is consistent, even 20 years ago to the present day, it's the same product with the same taste

tip for foreigners: if you order coffee or tea, it usually comes with condensed milk (so it is sweet)
there are some ordering guides online for you to customize your coffee or tea to your taste (search kopi.guide)
but some of the more common ones are
kopi-o (o means black, no milk)
kopi-o-kosong (black coffee + kosong, which means no sugar)
kopi-c (c means evaporated milk instead of condensed milk)

same thing for the kaya butter toast, if you are cutting calories, you can ask them to not include the butter or swap to a different spread

The yellow/orange one is the original one. The color sort of depends of what type of eggs is use. The Yellow Yoke and Orange / Red Yoke will affect the color of the final product. 
The Green one is add Pandan to it. 
The Brown one is Gula Melaka added to it but the Gula Melaka can be too dark, if you can get your hands on Corn Syrup. The Brown will not be too intense.

author: @sarahlim423
text: Okay, I love the video and the editing, however, the recipe is awful. Kaya is typically made with whole eggs and cooked for an extremely long time, so this is kind of like a cheat, quick method. This means the results are not the same as real authentic kaya. When I made this today, it was looking great until the very end. The texture was not right, it was more like a thick and gloopy caramel, and the taste was just extremely eggy. I guess that is what you would expect from an easier quicker method, but I was hoping for something way better. As well as that, the recipe only fills up half a jar, not a whole one. Would I recommend this recipe? No, probably not. Only if you are looking for a quick recipe providing eggy and gloopy results. If you really want a proper, authentic kaya taste, this is not the recipe for you.

author: @MelvinSimKH
text:
The soy sauce for the eggs is dark soy, not sweet soy. It’s still a little salty but it’s more caramelised so the saltiness doesn’t quite come through. It is used to lend a darker colour to food and also a richer taste. 

Sweet sauce or kicap manis is quite different in that it is primarily sweet in flavour. If you try char kway teow in Singapore (not Penang as they don’t use sweet sauce for theirs), you’ll get a good taste of the sweet soy there. Char kway teow is very popular in Singapore but it doesn’t get as much press as chicken rice does.

author: @khinweepang
text:
Nice to see your videos around Singapore! Do come here more often, I've been enjoying your videos a lot!
A gentle side note, "prata" (the Singapore name) is the localised name for "parotta", the original name of the refined flour, ghee-fried, stretched, layered, flaky bread from Chennai, Tamil Nadu,  South India.
Not to be confused with "paratha" or "parata", which is basically a non-layered, whole-wheat tortilla-like fried bread with a potato filling, from North India. Very different from "prata".

Their dough is very different. Prata is slap-stretched and folded. Paratha, being whole-wheat, is rolled with a rolling pin like stiff bread dough, not unlike tortillas which are pressed. 


Another fun fact, the Malaysian name for prata is "roti canai" (read as "roti chennai"), which simply means Chennai bread.

text:
I’m Singaporean, I can safely tell everyone that’s not based in SG who doesn’t know this, that our eggs are safe to be consumed raw or even when it’s this runny. All our eggs are pasteurised and undergo strict tests to ensure it is safe for our consumption! If they contain salmonella they are rejected and if they have already been released into the market, they will do a public recall of the product with the batch number etc and will ask those that have purchased to return the item as well.

Besides that, I’ve eaten soft boiled eggs with kaya/butter toast at toast box/ya kun and at our usual hawker centres but my opinion is that hawkers do it best! Love spamming soya sauce in it, mixing it up and drinking the eggs straight from the bowl, followed by the toast dry or with tea.

Great video, Singapore is a country where I see many good reviews and I’m glad you’re eating what I consider the most homey breakfast meal although it’s not the conventional sunny or hard boiled egg

author: @codshotgunner
text:
1. pandan kaya is not the best pick, XO hainanese kaya is the best for kaya toast
2. bread must be toasted, it can be charred to personal preference but it must be toasted so the butter can melt
3. eggs, soy and pepper needs to be mixed
4. while milo is a choice, coffee or tea is the main go to. Personally, i go coffee + small amount of condensed milk 

How much to dip to soak the bread in egg is entirely up to preference. some owners use a different type of bread so the amount of egg soaked changes, so dipping however much you want is the way to go but you want the part of toast you biting into to be completely covered

Also, a habit i picked up, you want some coffee left before finishing the toast so when you have left overs, you pour the hot coffee and mix with the eggs before drinking it all in a go. Maybe give this a try

author: @raymondetan7779
text:
新加坡在地人称它为半熟蛋。
咖椰酱有两种, 绿色的Kaya酱在制作时加入了斑兰叶, 所以呈现绿色及斑兰叶的香气。
褐色的Kaya酱俗称海南咖椰。
一般上两颗蛋的量只需加入半茶匙的黑酱油就可以了, 加太多会死咸。当然如果个人口味重的可以再加一 点, 但吃的太咸对健康不好。

author: @simplyme3306
text:
There are 2 versions of kaya. Green is because pandan juice is added. Whereas for the brown type (hainanese kaya), caramalised sugar is added and pandan leaves are cooked as whole leaves instead of juice.
However cheap commercial alternatives, especially the green coloured ones are just made with colouring and flavouring.
Ya Kun's bread toast is made extra thin by slicing the bread into half. I personally find it too dry and not much texture for their toast version. Prefer the steamed instead.
The soda cream crackers with kaya and butter is what the older generation eat. My father ate this way since he was a kid. Cream crackers with butter and kaya or sugar or jam.

新加坡平民美食早餐很多；有椰浆饭 （ NASI LEMAK ) ; 印度煎饼 （ ROTI PRATA ) ; 炒米粉；
猪肠粉 （ 米浆制的条状物 ）；炒罗卜糕 ；包点；笋粿；红龟粿；鸡蛋糕；豆浆油条；西式糕点土司等等；丰俭由人。
阿坤的套餐并不是普通新加坡人每天必吃的；抱歉；您只挑一家来介绍；会让广大的网民误会新加坡在地缺乏美食小吃。
您自己有烤面包机的话；早餐就能吃自烤面包；擦上加椰牛油再配一杯黑咖啡；就是一顿神仙早餐咯。
您不妨多尝尝新加坡多元种族不同的平民早餐小吃。

text:
这是阿坤的置入广告吗？我虽然不是新加坡建国一代，也在这片土地上生活了六十多年。新加坡人吃的早餐？别胡说八道了。这些年，阿坤在外国媒体买广告，造成国外的朋友，儍儍的以为阿坤卖的几片面包，和两粒半生熟的鸡蛋，就是新加坡人的主要早餐。如果真的那么好卖，阿坤也不用卖其他的食物了。
妳是华人，来新加坡也有几天了，难道妳不知道新加坡华人的主要早餐是面和粥吗，去小贩中心或食阁走走逛逛吧！
